prompt: You are testifying before the House Un-American Activities Committee (Cookout Division). It has been alleged that at the Petersons' potluck, you presented a store-bought dish in your own cookware. Respond to the committee.
response:
Mr. Chairman, distinguished members of the Cookout Division.

I appear before this committee today not to evade, but to clarify. I understand the gravity of the allegation that on July 14th, at the Petersons’ annual potluck, I presented a vessel of my own ceramic manufacture containing a product of industrial, store-bought origin. I do not deny the physical facts of this event. However, I categorically deny the *spirit* of the accusation.

Let the record show that the dish in question was a Marie Callender’s Four Cheese Pasta Bake. But let the record *also* show that it was transferred, while still at a safe internal temperature of 165 degrees Fahrenheit, into my grandmother’s hand-thrown stoneware casserole. This was not an act of deception, Mr. Chairman. It was an act of *thermal integrity and aesthetic solidarity*.

The Petersons’ gathering is a cornerstone of our neighborhood’s social fabric. To have arrived with a disposable aluminum tray and a plastic lid would have been an affront to the communal table. It would have signaled a laziness of spirit, a disregard for the unspoken covenant of the potluck: that we bring not merely calories, but *care*. My store-bought pasta bake was chosen after rigorous comparison of sodium content and cheese-to-noodle ratios. My grandmother’s dish was chosen because it retains heat and honors tradition. The marriage of the two was not subversion. It was *adaptation*.

Furthermore, I wish to address the whispered suggestion that this constitutes a “bait-and-switch” tactic akin to un-American culinary agitation. Mr. Chairman, is it un-American to seek efficiency without sacrificing presentation? Is it un-American to recognize one’s own limitations in scratch-made béchamel while still desiring to contribute to the collective feast? I submit that true patriotism at the potluck is measured not by the provenance of the ingredients, but by the sincerity of the contribution and the cleanliness of the vessel returned to the host.

I brought a dish. I brought it in appropriate attire. I labeled it clearly with an index card denoting both contents and allergens. I ate my portion. I complimented Mrs. Peterson’s deviled eggs. I took home my own cookware, washed.

If seeking to balance honest convenience with respectful presentation makes me suspect in the eyes of this committee, then I stand ready to accept your judgment. But I will not apologize for ensuring that even a humble, factory-assembled pasta bake was afforded the dignity of real stoneware at the Petersons’ table.

I yield my time, and I trust the committee will find my conduct consistent with the highest traditions of American potluck fellowship.
